question: How a 2001 study revealed that our visual expectations can overwrite our sense of smell when enology students described a dyed white wine using red wine words.

facts.fact: Frédéric Brochet was a PhD candidate at the University of Bordeaux II.
facts.quote: Nobody remembers the 2001 winner of Amorim Academy's annual competition... but many do recall the runner-up: a certain dissertation by Frédéric Brochet, then a PhD candidate at the University of Bordeaux II in Talence, France.

facts.fact: The experiment was part of his dissertation researching perception and wine tasting.
facts.quote: The study, conducted by Frédéric Brochet in 2001, was part of a larger dissertation on perception and wine tasting, which largely consisted of lexical analysis of published wine reviews using computer software.

facts.fact: Brochet and his team colored a white Bordeaux wine red using two grams per liter of natural grape anthocyanins.
facts.quote: They colored part of the white with grape anthocyanins, the natural pigment that makes red wine red, at 2 grams per liter.

facts.fact: Prior to the main test, the researchers verified that the pigment added no smell by having fifty people smell the plain and dyed wines in opaque glasses under red light.
facts.quote: First they checked the dye. Fifty people tasted the colored and plain white side by side in opaque glasses under red light, in a standard three-glass test, to confirm the pigment added no smell of its own.

facts.fact: During the first session of the experiment, 54 enology undergraduates smelled a real white and real red wine side-by-side, creating a list of smell words for each.
facts.quote: Then came the main test, with 54 undergraduates from the Bordeaux enology faculty, half men and half women, in two sessions a week apart. In the first, each student compared the real white and the real red in clear glasses under white light, built a personal list of smell words, and marked which wine showed each one more strongly.

facts.fact: A week later, the students were given the plain white wine and the same wine dyed red, and were asked to evaluate them using the list of words they had generated.
facts.quote: In the second, each student got the same list back, with no wine names on it, and compared the plain white with the white dyed red.

facts.fact: The panel of students described the odor of the artificially colored white wine as if it were a red wine.
facts.quote: A white wine artificially colored red with an odorless dye was olfactory described as a red wine by a panel of 54 tasters.

facts.fact: The researchers concluded that visual information dominates over olfactory information, causing the tasters to rely on the wine's color to describe its smell.
facts.quote: Hence, because of the visual information, the tasters discounted the olfactory information.

facts.fact: The study was widely picked up by the press and used to argue that wine tasting is nonsense.
facts.quote: The research, later published in the journal Brain and Language, is now widely used to show why wine tasting is total BS.

people.name: Frédéric Brochet
people.role: A PhD candidate in enology at the University of Bordeaux II
people.stake: His doctoral dissertation rested on proving that human perception of flavor is heavily manipulated by cognitive representation and visual cues.

timeline.what: Brochet and his team colored a white wine using grape anthocyanins and had fifty people confirm in a blind test under red light that the pigment added no smell.
timeline.why: To ensure that any difference in perception during the main test would be caused solely by the visual color of the wine, not by the dye's scent.

timeline.what: During the first session, 54 enology undergraduates smelled a real white and a real red wine side-by-side and generated a personal list of descriptive smell words.
timeline.why: To establish the baseline smell vocabulary each student naturally used when evaluating wines of known colors.

timeline.what: The students returned for a second session where they were asked to compare the plain white wine and the white wine dyed red using the smell words they had written the week before.
timeline.why: To test whether the visual appearance of the red dye would cause them to map their previously established red-wine odor descriptors onto a chemically white wine.

turn.what: The tasters described the artificially colored white wine using red wine words, leading the researchers to conclude that visual expectations override smell. The study was later widely publicized and misused by critics to argue that wine tasting is nonsense.

key_objects: A white Bordeaux wine from the 1996 vintage
Odorless grape anthocyanins used as red dye
Personal lists of smell descriptor words
unverified: The participants in the experiment were professional 'wine experts' (they were actually undergraduate enology students).
The wine was dyed using generic artificial red food coloring (it was colored with natural grape anthocyanins).
The experiment proved wine tasters cannot tell the difference between red and white wine by taste (the study specifically tested only olfactory descriptions, not full taste).
